# Judith Chapter 3 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 10

---

## Disagreement 1 — Verse 3:1: Who sends the messengers?

**EMET:** "And they-sent messengers to him for words of peace" — subject is implied, referring back to the coastal peoples of ch. 2.
**LOGOS:** "The nations sent messengers to him with words of peace."
**PNEUMA:** "One after another, the nations sent peace delegations to Holofernes." (Adds "one after another" and names Holofernes explicitly.)
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The plural subject is clear from context. PNEUMA's "one after another" implies sequence not stated in the Greek. "Messengers" (πρέσβεις) is preferable to "delegations" as more literal.

---

## Disagreement 2 — Verse 3:2: "lie prostrate before you"

**EMET:** "lie-prostrate before-you."
**LOGOS:** "we lie prostrate before you."
**PNEUMA:** "We throw ourselves before you."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Lie prostrate" is the standard English rendering of πίπτομεν ἐνώπιόν σου and carries the appropriate formal submission register. PNEUMA's "throw ourselves" is more vivid but less precise.

---

## Disagreement 3 — Verse 3:3: "buildings" vs. "estates"

**EMET:** "our-buildings and every-[piece-of] land of-ours."
**LOGOS:** "our estates and all our land."
**PNEUMA:** "Our estates, our land, our fields."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek οἰκοπεδεία can mean dwellings/buildings or estates/properties. "Estates" (LOGOS) captures the broader property sense better than "buildings" (EMET) in a context where agricultural land follows immediately. PNEUMA's truncation loses structure.

---

## Disagreement 4 — Verse 3:3: Inventory of possessions

**EMET:** Preserves all items as listed: wheat-fields, flocks, herds, tent-folds.
**LOGOS:** "wheat fields... flocks... herds... encampments of our tents."
**PNEUMA:** "our fields, our flocks, our herds, our encampments — everything is yours. Take it all."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The complete inventory should be preserved — it rhetorically conveys total capitulation. PNEUMA's "everything is yours. Take it all." adds interpretive summary not in the Greek.

---

## Disagreement 5 — Verse 3:6: "auxiliaries" vs. "allies"

**EMET:** "chosen men as auxiliaries."
**LOGOS:** "chosen men as allies."
**PNEUMA:** "drafted their best fighting men into his auxiliary forces."
**SOPHIA ruling:** EMET/PNEUMA. The Greek σύμμαχοι means "allies/fellow-fighters" — those fighting alongside, not merely auxiliary support troops. LOGOS's "allies" is accurate. However, the context of being "taken from" (ἔλαβεν) a conquered people implies something closer to auxiliaries or conscripts than willing allies. LOGOS "allies" adopted with note.

---

## Disagreement 6 — Verse 3:7: Reception with celebrations

**EMET:** "with garlands and with dances and with tambourines."
**LOGOS:** "with garlands and dances and tambourines."
**PNEUMA:** "with flowers and music and dancing — garlands, tambourines, celebrations."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The tripartite list (garlands, dances, tambourines) should be preserved. PNEUMA doubles up with "flowers and music and dancing — garlands, tambourines" which is redundant. "Celebrations" has no Greek basis.

---

## Disagreement 7 — Verse 3:8: "tore down their borders" vs. "frontier shrines"

**EMET:** "he-tore-down all their borders."
**LOGOS:** "He tore down their frontier shrines."
**PNEUMA:** "He demolished their border sanctuaries."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS/PNEUMA. The Greek ὅρια can mean "borders/boundaries" or "boundary markers" — in context following sacred groves, these are likely border sanctuaries/shrines (the LXX often uses ὅρια for territorial markers including sacred ones). "Frontier shrines" (LOGOS) is a reasonable interpretive rendering; "border sanctuaries" (PNEUMA) is equivalent. LOGOS adopted.

---

## Disagreement 8 — Verse 3:8: "all their tongues and all their tribes would call upon him as god"

**EMET:** "all-their tongues and all-their tribes would-call-upon him as god."
**LOGOS:** "all their tongues and all their tribes would invoke him as god."
**PNEUMA:** "every tongue, every tribe, calling his name as divine."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Invoke him as god" is precise for ἐπικαλεῖσθαι αὐτὸν θεόν. PNEUMA's "calling his name as divine" is slightly weaker — the Greek "as god" (θεόν, noun) is stronger than "as divine" (adjective). This is a key theological moment of Nebuchadnezzar's divine pretension; precision matters.

---

## Disagreement 9 — Verse 3:9: Geography — "faces the great ridge"

**EMET:** "near Dothan which faces the-great ridge of Judea."
**LOGOS:** "near Dothan, which faces the great ridge of Judea."
**PNEUMA:** "near Dothan, within sight of the great ridge that marks the approach to Judea."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Which faces the great ridge of Judea" preserves the directional orientation of the Greek κατέναντι τοῦ μεγάλου αὐχένος Ιουδαίας. PNEUMA's "within sight of" is interpretive; "marks the approach" is an explanatory addition.

---

## Disagreement 10 — Verse 3:10: "one month of days" and purpose

**EMET:** "he-was-there one-month of-days, in-order-to gather all-the supplies of his army."
**LOGOS:** "remained there a full month, gathering all the supplies of his army."
**PNEUMA:** "settled in between Geba and Scythopolis for a full month, restocking his supply lines before the next push."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "A full month" renders μῆνα ἡμερῶν (literally "a month of days") well. LOGOS's "gathering all the supplies" is accurate. PNEUMA's "restocking his supply lines" is modern military language; "before the next push" adds narrative framing not in the text.
